items.title: AI Agents Are Where Humans Were 70,000 Years Ago
items.summary: In episode 1041 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Dr. Vijoy Pandey, SVP/GM Outshift by Cisco, how AI agents are currently at a stage comparable to human intelligence 70,000 years ago, just before the cognitive revolution. They explore the concept of the "Internet of Cognition" and how connecting these agents will lead to a collective intelligence, mirroring humanity's journey from individual to collective intelligence. This fascinating comparison highlights the potential for a new era of AI development. Production note: this episode was recorded before the Internet of Cognition software shipped, so a few names changed between recording and release. OXP is now SCOPE — System for Cognitive Observability, Provenance & Explainability. ACCORD and CONCORD are the protocol names, not acronyms (Vijoy calls them acronyms in the episode). All three: github.com/ioc-project

items.title: Can Robots Learn to Work Together? (with Vijoy Pandey)
items.summary: In Episode #1041, Dr. Vijoy Pandey (SVP and General Manager of Outshift, Cisco's incubation engine) returns for a third visit to explain why multi-agent systems fail without anyone noticing. Agents from different vendors, clouds and organisations can now exchange perfectly valid messages, but connection is not cognition: they do not agree on what those messages mean. Vijoy's team analyzed multi-agent sessions from its own production deployments and from public traces, and found a cognitive failure in every single one. In this episode, he lays out the kinds of failure he sees and how fast they compound, introduces the open-source observability platform and protocols Outshift has shipped to catch and correct drift mid-task, details a record-breaking quantum network running on real New York City fiber, and explains why probabilistic AI software running on deterministic hardware is a mismatch worth fixing. Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/1041

items.title: AI Is Replacing Junior Employees
items.summary: Here's how I think about first jobs. You do the basic work, someone more experienced checks it, and the company gets useful work while you learn. If AI can do that work, a company may have less reason to pay you to practice. Economists explored this in one model of training. It's a model, so it doesn't prove training will disappear. Still, who pays for those early years of learning is an open question. How did you learn the hard parts of your job?
